Zillah
ZIL-lah
n. (proper, a wife of Lamech; Hebrew, shadow)
Hebrew Tsillah, from tsel, a shadow. She is one of the two wives of Lamech the Cainite, and her appearance marks the first polygamy recorded in Scripture and the first boast of vengeance.

Biblical Definition

The line of Cain reaches its climax in a man with two wives: “And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah” (Genesis 4:19). This is the first departure from the one flesh of Genesis 2 that Scripture records, and it is recorded in the line of the murderer. Zillah's son is the father of metallurgy: “And Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubalcain was Naamah” (Genesis 4:22). Then Lamech gathers both wives to hear a poem: “And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt” (Genesis 4:23), and he claims a vengeance seventy and sevenfold. Civilization's first arts — cattle, music, metal — and its first boast of unlimited revenge belong to the same household and the same chapter.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the two wives of Lamech in the line of Cain, and the mother of Tubal-cain.

expand to see more

POLYGAMY, n. A plurality of wives or husbands at the same time.

VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offense; retribution.

ARTIFICER, n. An artist; a mechanic or manufacturer; one whose occupation requires skill or knowledge of a particular kind.

SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light, apparent on a plane.

BRASS, n. An alloy of copper and zinc; in Scripture, often copper or bronze, wrought from the earliest times.

Key Scripture

Genesis 4:19 — "And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah."

Genesis 4:22 — "And Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubalcain was Naamah."

Genesis 4:23 — "And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt. I"

Genesis 4:24 — "If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold."

Modern Corruption

Technological advance is treated as moral advance, and Genesis 4 places the first metallurgy, the first music and the first polygamy in the same household as the first boast of unlimited revenge.

expand to see more

The story civilization tells about itself is that skill and progress travel together, so that a more capable society is a better one. Genesis 4 is arranged to deny it. In the line of Cain come tents and cattle, the harp and the organ, and every artificer in brass and iron — real goods, common grace, and Scripture does not sneer at any of them. In the same chapter, the same household and the same generation come the first plural marriage and Lamech's song, in which a man boasts of killing a young man for wounding him and claims a vengeance seventy and sevenfold. Capability increased; the heart did not change.

Our Lord answered that song directly. When Peter asked whether he should forgive seven times, Christ replied until seventy times seven — taking Lamech's number for vengeance and turning it into the measure of forgiveness. That is the gospel's reply to the line of Cain. Zillah and Adah were summoned to hear a boast of blood; the church is called to hear a word of pardon that runs to the same limit and beyond it, because the blood of Christ speaketh better things than that of Abel.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Tsillah (H6741), shadow; tsel (H6738), a shadow; Tuwbal Qayin (H8423), Tubal-cain; naqam (H5358), to avenge.

expand to see more

Hebrew Tsillah (H6741) — Zillah, shadow; one of the two wives of Lamech.

Hebrew tsel (H6738) — a shadow, a shade; the root of her name.

Hebrew Adah (H5711) — Adah, ornament; the other wife, mother of Jabal and Jubal.

Hebrew Tuwbal Qayin (H8423) — Tubal-cain; instructer of every artificer in brass and iron.

Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge, to take vengeance; Lamech's seventy and sevenfold.

Usage

"“The name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah” — the first polygamy."

"“Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain” — the first worker in brass and iron."

"“Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech” — the first boast of vengeance."
